title: High Prevalence of Misinformation Found in YouTube Prostate Cancer Videos
screen_reason: Not a primary study. The record (DOI 10.1097/01.cot.0000553127.66951.40) is a journalistic news feature in Oncology Times, written by a contributing writer (Kelly Wolfgang), reporting on and interviewing the lead author of a SEPARATE primary study — Loeb et al., European Urology 2018, doi.org/10.1016/j.eururo.2018.10.056 — which is explicitly cited in the text. Two independent grounds for exclusion: (1) §1 excludes commentary/journalism; there is no method, no sampling frame and no analysis of the author's own; (2) R8 forbids keeping a figure the paper cites from elsewhere, and EVERY quantitative value here ('over 75 percent', '115 of those', '25% biased toward new technology', '19 percent recommended complementary or alternative medicine', DISCERN-derived shares) belongs to Loeb et al. and is reported second-hand.
missed_or_uncertain:
ADJUDICATOR: this is the judgement call of the batch, and it needs a decision at corpus level, not row level. If the review treats this record as a pointer to the underlying primary study rather than as a study in its own right, the extractable figure is: 115 of the top 150 prostate cancer screening/treatment videos on YouTube contained biased or misinformative content (76.7%), source_quote 'The study examined the top 150 videos on prostate screening and treatment, with a combined total of over 1.3 million views, finding that 115 of those contained biased information, ranging from alternative medicine recommendations that are not evidence-based to outdated professional recommendations.' — a CONTENT row, YouTube, USA/global, curated top-N search corpus, topic health_other, researcher_coding against USPSTF/professional guidelines plus DISCERN. If Loeb et al. (Eur Urol 2018) is ALREADY in the corpus under its own id, including this record too would double-count the same 150 videos, so the two records must not both contribute a poolable row.

A SEPARATE WARNING about this text as a source: it contains an outright factual error about its own headline number. It says 'A recent study found that the platform houses over 600,000 videos on the topic of prostate cancer alone ... and over 75 percent of those videos included misinformative content'. The 75% does NOT apply to the 600,000; the next sentence makes clear the study examined only the TOP 150 videos, of which 115 (76.7%) contained biased information. Anyone extracting from this news piece rather than from Loeb et al. risks recording a 75% prevalence against a denominator of 600,000+ videos, which is roughly 4,000 times too large and would badly distort a prevalence pool.

Other second-hand figures in the text, all quality-flavoured rather than falsity-based and all belonging to Loeb et al.: 75% of videos gave a moderate-to-good description of benefits vs 53% for harms; about half provided moderate-to-good support for shared decision-making; 'A quarter of videos were biased toward the use of new technology and 19 percent recommended complementary or alternative medicine'; 5 of 150 videos were authored by patients; Flesch-Kincaid reading level 12th grade; a subset of 50 videos graded on PEMAT; total reach over 6 million viewers across videos and comments; one video with more than 300,000 views recommended injecting herbal supplements into the prostate. Note that the instrument described is DISCERN plus custom rankings including 'the extent of misinformation', so even the primary study mixes a QUALITY instrument with an explicit misinformation rating — worth checking against the primary text if the review decides to include Loeb et al.

On text_status: the file header labels this 'ABSTRACT ONLY', and I have recorded abstract_only to match, but the retrieved text is in fact the complete news article, not an abstract. It is also NOT the paper a reader would expect from the title's framing of 'a study'.

rob.design: No design of its own. Magazine news feature reporting a third-party cross-sectional content analysis (Loeb et al., European Urology 2018) of the top 150 YouTube videos returned for 'prostate cancer screening' and 'prostate cancer treatment', graded with the DISCERN instrument plus custom items (intended audience, favouring new technology, complementary/alternative medicine, commercial bias, extent of misinformation), with a 50-video subset graded on Flesch-Kincaid reading level and the AHRQ PEMAT. Sampling depth, coder count, coder training and intercoder reliability for that primary study are not reported here; none can be appraised from this text.
rob.item6_quote: The study also included rankings on intended audience, favoring new technology, recommending complementary/alternative medicine, commercial bias, and the extent of misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: The study examined the top 150 videos on prostate screening and treatment, with a combined total of over 1.3 million views, finding that 115 of those contained biased information, ranging from alternative medicine recommendations that are not evidence-based to outdated professional recommendations.
